summary: A character-level language model trained in the browser on a small built-in text. The visitor sets how many previous characters the model can see (context length), types a prompt to see the predicted next-character probabilities, generates text with a temperature control, and compares training and held-out bits per character for every context length.
use_for: language models, NLP, sequence modelling, transformers, attention, recurrent networks, tokenization, text generation, context length, next-token prediction, translation
one_liner: Train a tiny language model live; change how much context it sees and watch its predictions sharpen.
mechanism: The demo shows the core job of every language model: predict the next symbol from the ones before it. This model just counts which character follows each short context in a small text, so you can see exactly how much more context helps, and where it starts memorising instead of generalising.
try: Slide context length from 1 to 5 and press Generate each time. The output goes from letter soup to word-like fragments to whole copied phrases.
Type the start of a word in the prompt box and watch the next-character bars. Longer context makes the prediction much more confident.
Compare the two bar charts. Training bits per character keeps falling as context grows, while held-out text stops improving: longer contexts are seen too rarely to generalise.
Raise the temperature to make sampling more random, or lower it toward 0 for the single most likely continuation.
simplifications: The model is a counting n-gram model with Witten–Bell smoothing on a few kilobytes of text, not a neural network. It shows the prediction task and the role of context, but not how neural models generalise across similar contexts.
It works on single characters with a fixed, short context window. Modern models use subword tokens, learn which earlier tokens matter, and train on billions of words.
